title: Token tiling throughput experiments
content:
Purpose:
Quick working notes for a novel family of throughput/quality tradeoff experiments: token-level tiling + stochastic context eliding. Goal is to quantify latency and cost savings against quality regressions for model onboarding (esp. long-context assistant prompts) and to generate concrete guardrails for rollout policies (canary thresholds, allowed quality delta).

Background / motivation:
- We often see large variance in per-request token counts due to optional system/user context (examples, tool docs, conversation history). Static max_tokens and batching alone do not capture the structure: many requests include repeated common prefix blocks (instruction + 2 example pairs) that contribute to KV cache warmups but have predictable impact on output.
- Existing experiments (batch/cache/max_tokens sweeps) are great but treat input as monolithic. Token tiling attempts to split input into: core_tile (required minimal prompt), optional_tiles (examples, long context blobs), and streaming tiles (long references). By dynamically deciding which tiles to send to the model at request time (based on probability / utility heuristics) we can reduce tokens per inference while preserving quality for the majority of cases.

Key idea (stochastic context eliding):
- For each optional tile we compute a small heuristic score (similarity to user intent embedding, token overlap with prompt, or importance classifier).
- If score < threshold t, we drop that tile when sending request (server-side) OR we send a compressed sentinel ("<<ELIDED_EXAMPLE_N>>") and rely on model generalization.
- We sweep t from 0.0 (send everything) to 0.9 (send only highest-scoring optional tiles). We pair that with batching policies and prefix/KV caching TTLs to measure combined effects.

Experiment matrix (overview):
- Models: base-open-xxl-8bit, open-rtl-1.9B-quant, redwood-v1-small (for reference).
- Batching configs: static batch sizes {1, 4, 16, 64}, continuous batching window {10ms, 50ms, 200ms}.
- Cache configs: prefix cache OFF, prefix cache ON (in-memory, TTLs {30s, 5min}), prefix cache with evict-on-size {500MB}.
- Max_tokens: model-side max_generation {64, 256, 1024} (to capture truncation effects).
- Tiling thresholds t: [0.0, 0.1, 0.25, 0.5, 0.75, 0.9].
- Traffic profile: synthetic mixture (70% short prompts < 200 tokens, 20% medium 200-800 tokens, 10% long > 800). Also replay of production request traces (anonymized) from two customers for a subset.

Metrics captured (per-config):
- Latency: p50, p90, p95 server-side wall-clock for first-token and end-to-end.
- Throughput: tokens/sec per GPU and requests/sec tail.
- Cost proxy: tokens emitted + tokens sent (ingress) aggregated to derive estimated $/1M tokens using hosted pricing assumptions.
- Quality: automatic metrics over a gold promptset (50 hand-curated cases) — ROUGE-L for summarization-like tasks, exact-match / BLEU variants for instruction tasks, and a small human eval on 300 sampled outputs (3 raters).
- Regression detector: delta_F1 and human pass-rate (binary accept/reject) compared to baseline (t=0.0, prefix-cache=ON/TTL=5min, batch=16, max_tokens=256).

Preliminary findings (high-level):
- Small to moderate thresholds (t=0.1-0.25) provided substantial token savings (~12-18% tokens_in per request) with negligible median latency impact and <1.5% drop in auto-metrics on our onboarding promptset. Human accept rate drop was within noise for most assistant tasks.
- Larger thresholds (t>=0.5) hit diminishing returns for tokens sent but began to expose quality regressions on multi-example instruction tasks (eg. chain-of-thought-like examples). Regression detected at t=0.5: human pass-rate down ~6-9% for the long-context cases.
- Prefix cache TTL interacts strongly: with TTL=5min we saw warm-cache hit rates >92% for common prefixes and tiling savings compounded (effective per-request tokens reduced up to 28%). With TTL=30s cache churn increased and tiling savings mostly offset by recaching overhead.
- Batching tradeoffs: continuous batching windows of 50ms gave the best end-to-end throughput/latency compromise for mixed traffic. Static large batches (64) improved raw GPU throughput but increased p95 latency so much that canary SLOs would have been violated for interactive endpoints.
- Max_tokens low caps (64) caused quality truncation in ~4% of our gold cases for long-answer tasks; tiling propagates this risk because a trimmed context may force more generation tokens. Important to ensure model-side generation budget remains sufficient before aggressive eliding.

Micro-observations and oddities (raw notes):
- One dataset customer had a heavy skew: 35% of traffic included the same 3-example prefix; prefix-cache with tiling removed almost all repeated sends and yielded >40% cost reduction for that customer under moderate t.
- When we elided examples and replaced them with a sentinel token, some model variants hallucinated content by inventing example labels — more common in smaller models. Larger models were robust to the sentinel trick.
- Latency improvements on p95 were surprisingly sensitive to scheduler fairness: when we prioritized low token-count requests we improved overall p95 but increased tail for long ones. Need fairness policy if we want SLOs across classes.

Quality gating and recommended guardrails (draft):
- Canary policy: start with t=0.1 + prefix-cache TTL=5m + continuous batching 50ms on canary cluster for 48h; require human pass-rate >= baseline - 2% and automated metric delta <= -1.0 absolute on primary evalset.
- Rollout ramp: 0% -> 10% -> 33% -> 66% -> 100% over rolling 7-day windows with automated rollback on sustained p95 uplift > 20ms or human pass-rate drop >3%.
- Max_tokens lower bounds: avoid lowering generation cap below baseline 256 for tasks requiring long-form output unless a separate truncation policy is in place.

Open questions / next steps:
- Utility estimator: the heuristic we used (cosine on small embeddings) worked but false-negatives (dropping useful example) were costly. Can we train a tiny binary classifier (on the onboarding promptset) to predict when an optional tile is critical?
- Per-customer policies: for customers with heavy repeated prefixes, we should expose a per-customer aggressive elide mode. Need to measure security/PII implications of eliding and caching.
- Stability across model variants: run same sweep on dedicated-prod GPU types (A100 vs H100 equivalents) — kernel selection and compilation might change latency/cost interplay when tiles change typical sequence lengths.
- Integration: prototype required server-side decision point in request pipeline (pre-router) that computes tile scores cheaply (<=1ms). Evaluate overhead.

Notes to self / action items:
- Run deterministic replay for customer A traces with t in {0.1, 0.25, 0.5} using open-rtl-1.9B-quant and record latency traces (JIRA-MLINF-732 assigned).
- Add small labeling job for 2k examples to train tile-utility classifier (Priya to coordinate).
- Create a minimal canary PR adding elide toggles to runtime (Omar) and run internal A/B for 48h on dev cluster (PR: github.com/redwood-inference/tiling-experiments/pull/12).

Appendix: short checklist for reproducing experiment locally
- Dataset: onboarding_gold_v3 (50 gold cases) + customer_replay_A (anonymized).
- Configs stored: s3://redwood-experiments/tiling/configs/ (note: need permissions) — include batcher, cache TTL, tiling thresholds.
- Eval harness: scripts/run_tiling_sweep.py (see PR above)

End of working notes. This doc is intentionally informal; will excerpt into a cleaned onboarding-tiling-brief once we have deterministic replay results and human evals consolidated.
